name: Water-powered trip-hammers in Han China
summary: By the Han dynasty Chinese millers used a water wheel to work a row of tilt-hammers for hulling grain, mechanising a pounding task earlier done by hand or foot.
description: A Han dynasty glazed funerary model of a grain mill in the Hong Kong Heritage Museum has a water channel, water gates and a bracket for a vertical wheel whose horizontal shaft, now missing, drove three pestles; Shi Xiaolei reads it as a battery of hydraulic tilt hammers. The foot-worked forerunner is described by Huan Tan in the Xin Lun, around the first years AD, as ten times as productive as the hand pestle. The sources read do not show when within the Han period water-driven hammers first appeared.

impact.note: Water-driven hammers were used across China for centuries for grain and later clay and paper pulp (reach 2), a large saving of labour on a task already done by hand and foot (depth 1), with a few direct successors such as combined hammer-and-mill works (generativity 1); depth lowered from the lead's 2.

date.label: around the beginning years of AD
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Writing in the years between the two Han dynasties, around the first years AD, Huan Tan says in the Xin Lun that the treadle-operated tilt hammer is ten times as productive as the hand pestle; this is the foot-worked forerunner, not the water-driven hammer.

evidence.supports: The advantage of the treadle-operated tilt hammer is ten times as productive as the pestle by hands because it gets the help from the weight of the laborer

date.label: Han dynasty (202 BCE to 220 CE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: A funerary model of a grain mill, dated by the source only to the Han dynasty, shows a water-driven battery of tilt hammers working beside a mill and a winnowing fan.

evidence.supports: There is a green glazed grain funerary ware mill model of Han Dynasty(fig.3) in the collection of the Hongkong Heritage Museum, which shows the working condition of a battery « hydraulic tilt hammer and other machines
evidence.locator: Text accompanying Fig. 3, as rendered on the Academia.edu page (the stray mark is in the page's own text)

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Huan Tan's Xin Lun is widely reported, after Needham (Science and Civilisation in China vol. 4 part 2), to go on to mention water power used for pounding; that passage was not found on a page that could be read and needs a source, since it would date water-driven hammers to about AD 20.
The date, provenance and find context of the Hong Kong Heritage Museum model need a source; its wheel and shaft are missing and its reading as water-driven is the author's.
Du Shi's water-powered bellows of AD 31 and the rival claims of Hellenistic and Roman cams and ore-stamping mills were not checked.
The Han dynasty's dates (202 BCE to 220 CE) are supplied from general knowledge; the source says only 'Han Dynasty'.

research.note: The sources read do not say whether Chinese hammers were independent of earlier pounding devices or derived from elsewhere.
